answer.label: Not Carl Jung — an unsourced modern fabrication
answer.authorDates: C. G. Jung, 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist, founder of analytical psychology
answer.sourceLine: This line is widely pinned on Jung across social media and quote sites, but it appears in none of his documented writings. Wikiquote lists it only under “Attributed” with no source ↗, Quote Investigator has never traced it, and its conspiratorial phrasing (“to maintain order and control you must isolate the intellectual”) reads as modern internet writing, not Jung. Treat it as a fabrication until a primary source surfaces.

author.name: Carl Jung
author.heading: Who Carl Jung actually was
author.metaLine: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist & founder of analytical psychology
author.bio: Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology, developing ideas such as the collective unconscious, archetypes, individuation, and psychological types. Because his name lends instant intellectual weight, it is one of the internet’s most common magnets for polished-sounding quotations he never wrote — and this line, absent from his Collected Works, appears to be one of them.

misattribution.heading: Why this is credited to Jung
misattribution.intro: The quote spread as image macros and social posts stamped with Jung’s name, then hardened into “fact” through repetition. No stage of that chain passes through an actual Jung text.

items.why: The exact phrasing is absent from Jung’s Collected Works, seminars, and letters; Wikiquote can only file it under “Attributed” ↗ with no citation.

Framing intellectuals as targets an unnamed power must “isolate” “to maintain order and control” is the vocabulary of modern anti-establishment memes, not of Jung’s analytical psychology, as skeptical readers note ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no evidence Carl Jung wrote or said this. It survives only as an unsourced attribution ↗ — treat it as a modern fabrication until a primary source is found.

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: Jung is a premier “quote magnet”: his reputation for depth makes any grave, aphoristic sentence sound plausibly his. A line about the persecuted deep thinker flatters the reader who shares it — casting them, implicitly, as the misunderstood sage — which is exactly the emotional engine that drives fabricated quotes to spread faster than sourced ones.

The honest position is narrow but firm: this specific wording cannot be found in anything Jung published, and no researcher has produced a primary source. That does not prove Jung opposed the sentiment; it means the sentence, as worded, is not his.
context.pull: Absent from every Jung text yet everywhere under his name — the signature of a quote magnet.
